newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Guinness - a not so Irish pint of stout.
newsitem.headline: Guinness - a not so Irish pint of stout.

text.p: Ireland's jet black stout with the famous creamy head was thrust into the news on Monday by the surprise 20-billion pound ($32.5 billion) merger between Guinness Plc and drinks giant Grand Metropolitan Plc.
After a history of more than 200 years the name Guinness is still considered by many Ireland's national drink, immortalised in poem and prose, most notably Ireland's James Joyce.
Yet the brewer has far outgrown its birthplace.
Arthur Guinness, in 1759, signed a 9,000 year lease at an annual rent of 45 Irish pounds ($70) per annum on a disused brewery in Dublin.
This brewery became the birthplace of Guinness stout ale.
At that time the Guinness brewery consisted of a copper, a mill, two malthouses, stables for 12 horses and a loft which could hold 200 tons of hay.
The first export shipment of Guinness -- 6.5 barrels -- left Dublin on a sailing ship in 1769, bound for England.

The St James's Gate brewery in Dublin is now one of five with sisters in Britain, Nigeria, Malaysia, Cameroun and Ghana. In 1997 almost 10 million glasses of Guinness are produced around the world every day.
The Guinness/Grand Metropolitan merger creates the world's seventh largest food and drinks company, GMG Brands, with combined sales of more than 100 million cases.

"The merger means quite a lot for the UK market but it means very little to Ireland," one Dublin analyst said. "Guinness is a British registered company with interests world-wide, all it has left in Ireland is the brewery."
Ironically analysts say the merger could be the catalyst that brings Guinness back to Ireland although they conceded it was a long shot.
They say the Guinness stout breweries may no longer fit it with the new company's growth path.
"It has been suggested that that GMG Brands will focus on the drinks side where they have a lot of potential synergies and may sell off the brewery," one analyst said.
The merger brings together brands such as Smirnoff vodka, Bailey's and Cinzano with Guinness-owned Johnnie Walker and Bell's Scotch whisky and Gordon's gin.
Guinness' Irish beer brewery may be a small part of this new group but it is still central to Irish life.

The Irish brewer spends about 200 million Irish pounds per annum in the Republic of Ireland. It employs a workforce of 2,300 and is indirectly responsible for another 30,000 jobs in a country with one in nine unemployed.

Guinness by-products from the company's brewing processes are sold directly to Irish farmers for animal feed and the excise duty and Value-Added-Tax on Guinness Ireland products contribute 350 million Irish pounds ($532 million) to the country's exchequer each year.
The 'black brew' is used as a symbol and an attraction of Ireland in most tourism promotions, a crucial industry to a country with little to offer in terms of natural resources except its beauty.
Guinness Ireland sponsors a myriad of cultural events in the country ranging from horse racing to jazz festivals.
While the group has become a world-wide conglomerate Ireland and Guinness remain synonymous in many people's minds.
($ = 0.657 Irish Pounds)
